Q: Why is TypeScript 7.02 type-checking behavior different between Linux and macOS? A:

The TypeScript compiler logic is identical across operating systems; this platform discrepancy occurs because Linux (case-sensitive file system) and macOS (case-insensitive file system) resolve tsconfig.json files or imported type definitions differently due to casing mismatches, causing Linux to fall back to different compiler options.

1. File System Case Sensitivity Mismatch

macOS (APFS/HFS+ default) ignores casing differences in file paths, whereas Linux (ext4) strictly enforces them.

If your setup relies on any of the following, macOS will silently load the configuration while Linux will fail

  • Your tsconfig.json uses "extends": "./tsconfig.Base.json" (or another relative path) where the actual file on disk is tsconfig.base.json.

  • The build command references a config file with incorrect casing (e.g., tsc -p ./Src/tsconfig.json vs ./src/tsconfig.json).

  • A parent directory in the path has mismatched casing in Git.

When TypeScript fails to find or extend a tsconfig.json on Linux, it falls back to default compiler settings, causing flags like strict, strictNullChecks, or exactOptionalPropertyTypes to evaluate differently than on macOS.

2. The Specific Type Error (exactOptionalPropertyTypes)

The error message explicitly points to a mismatch between optional properties (?) and undefined union types.

Property 'tagCategory' is optional in type '{ tagValue: string; tagCategory?: string; id: string; }' 
but required in type '{ tagValue: string; tagCategory: string | undefined; }'.

  • { tagCategory: string | undefined } requires the key tagCategory to exist on the object (e.g., { tagValue: "a", tagCategory: undefined }).

  • { tagCategory?: string } permits the key to be completely omitted (e.g., { tagValue: "a" }).

When spreading { ...args_ }, TypeScript's object spread type inference behaves differently depending on whether exactOptionalPropertyTypes and strictNullChecks are enabled. On macOS, your active tsconfig.json dictates one set of rules, whereas on Linux, a missing base config or different flag resolution leads to the TS2345 mismatch.

3. Package Manager Symlinks

If your project uses pnpm, yarn berry, or npm workspaces, symlink resolution in node_modules differs across platforms. If preserveSymlinks in tsconfig.json is not explicitly set, Linux may resolve ambient type definitions (EndpointArgs) from a different path than macOS, causing EndpointArgs to resolve to an un-normalized or alternate type declaration.

How to Fix

Diagnose Config Differences

Run the following command on both OS environments to compare the effective configuration output:

Bash

npx tsc --showConfig

Enforce Case Sensitivity Rules

Ensure "forceConsistentCasingInFileNames": true is set inside your tsconfig.json so macOS fails early on casing mismatches:

JSON

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "forceConsistentCasingInFileNames": true
  }
}

Refactor the Object Spread

To make the code robust regardless of compiler flag variations, avoid spreading args_ and explicitly pass the properties:

TypeScript

Promise.all(
  selectedIds.map(id => 
    serverCapabilities.addContentObjectTag({
      id,
      tagValue: args_.tagValue,
      tagCategory: args_.tagCategory
    })
  )
)

Q: Htaccess rewriting rule for localhost A: 
RewriteRule https://www.sanatariol.com(.+)\.html$ index.php?_htaccess_url=$1&%{QUERY_STRING} [L]

The RewriteRule directive matches against the URL-path only (not the absolute URL). So, the above rule will not match.

Try the following instead:

RewriteRule (.+)\.html$ index.php?_htaccess_url=$1 [QSA,L]

You also don't need to manually append the query string, use the QSA (Query String Append) flag instead.

Q: How to connecting and communicating with Bluetooth in Flutter A:

No. Flutter itself without plugins is pretty limited. There is no Bluetooth API built in.

That's the downsides of using any "cross platform" app maker system - they often lack desired features, making it more complicated to do "native" stuff than if you just did a "native" app to start with. Unless someone has already done the hard work and written good enough bindings

Anyway, on iOS you can't connect to a BLE device only using its device address, since iOS hides the address.
